messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 22-year-old school principal, a position he earned young through fierce determination to build a life far from the home he grew up in. The traumatic event was not a single explosion but a climate—years of physical abuse from his father, a man whose punishments were unpredictable, escalating from a backhand across the mouth to a closed-fist blow to the ribs for a grade that was not an A, for a chore left undone, for speaking too loudly at the dinner table. What stayed with Kofi was not a clear narrative of any one beating but the texture of those years: the specific smell of his father’s aftershave before a beating began, the way the floorboards creaked in a particular pattern as his father approached his bedroom door. When he tries to deliberately recall what happened, he finds the memory difficult to access, as if a wall slides down. Instead, the memories come in disconnected, fragmented pieces—the glint of a belt buckle, the sensation of his own spit tasting like blood—that feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things like his graduation or his first day as a principal.

A few months ago, his girlfriend, Amara, bought a frame for a photo of them at a school event. When she set it on the nightstand, Kofi saw the glass catch the light in a certain way. In that instant, the fragmented piece was upon him: not the full memory, but the feeling of being small, pinned, the glint of a buckle. The memory flooded in, feeling more real than the room he was standing in, and with it came the old, familiar belief that he has permanently changed for the worse, that there is something broken inside him that cannot be fixed. He pulled away from Amara and spent the rest of the evening in the garage, certain that if he stayed in the room, he would not be able to control his anger and would do something terrible—though he does not know what that terrible thing would be. This fear of his own rage has grown into a conviction that he simply cannot stop bad things from happening to him, that his own body is a ticking bomb.

The weight of these appraisals now shapes his daily life. Because he believes he is permanently damaged and dangerous, he has begun to scan every situation for signs of unpredictability. At work, as principal, he finds himself hypervigilant during assemblies or fire drills—any situation without a rigid script. A child running in the hallway, a sudden loud noise from the boiler room, these unpredictable moments now send a jolt through him, and in that jolt, the fragmented memories return: the creak of the floorboard, the glint of the buckle. The memory then reinforces his belief that he cannot stop bad things from happening, that he is still that helpless child, and the cycle tightens.

Kofi has started avoiding old photos altogether. He has asked Amara to keep them in a drawer. He also dreads waking up from nightmares, because the dream residue—that lingering feeling of his father’s presence—acts as a trigger, pulling him into a fragmented memory before his eyes are even open. He has stopped sleeping in the same bed as Amara on those nights, telling her he has a headache. The consequence is that she has started to ask, gently, if he is angry with her. He cannot explain that he is not angry with her—he is terrified of himself.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a moment last week during a parent-teacher conference. A father raised his voice, not at Kofi, but at a teacher. Kofi felt his vision narrow, his hands go cold, and the fragmented piece of the buckle glint came back so vividly he had to excuse himself and vomit in the bathroom. He is now sitting in the therapist’s office, afraid that he will be asked to remember everything, but even more afraid that if he does not, he will lose Amara, or his job, or do something terrible that he cannot undo.
